query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A hybrid high-throughput strategy that integrates first-principles or CALPHAD-based thermodynamic modeling with targeted differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and dilatometry measurements can accurately and efficiently determine the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change upon melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties for a wide composition range of high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy specimens (single-phase or near-single-phase) with precisely controlled compositions, either in as-cast or homogenized form, prepared for thermal and structural characterization.
generation.intervention: Use advanced thermodynamic calculations (e.g., CALPHAD, ab initio methods) in synergy with minimal DSC and in-situ dilatometry trials to refine model parameters for each alloy composition, thereby calibrating predicted melting transitions and liquid-phase properties.
generation.conditions: Controlled experimental environment with heating rates (5–20 K/min) in DSC to capture melting transitions accurately, standard atmospheric pressure or inert atmosphere, and stable fixture conditions during dilatometry for volumetric change measurements.
generation.structural_mediator: Entropic stabilization from multiple principal elements in high-entropy alloys, resulting in sloped free-energy surfaces that can be screened by integrating theoretical models of mixing enthalpy and configurational entropy with partial experimental data.
generation.mechanism: Local chemical and topological disorder in multi-principal element alloys modifies the lattice vibrational entropy and enthalpy, which can be captured by combining thermodynamic modeling and direct thermal/volumetric measurements to predict bulk melting behavior and liquid-phase stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Melting temperature predictions accurate to ±10 K, enthalpies of fusion and entropies of fusion within ±5%, and volume changes upon melting determined with <5% deviation relative to direct experimental measurements, for multi-principal-element compositions near and at equiatomic concentrations.
generation.baseline: Existing empirical correlations or unrefined databases for high-entropy alloys often yield deviations of up to 20–30% for melting points and fusion parameters in complex compositions.
generation.boundary: Applicability is strongest for high-entropy alloys where minimal phase segregation is observed, typically single-phase or near-single-phase equiatomic or close-to-equiatomic alloys. Multi-phase or metastable compositions may exhibit larger uncertainties.
generation.uncertainty: Potential underestimation of experimental complexities (e.g., oxidation or partial reactions) and limitations in the thermodynamic databases when extrapolating beyond well-characterized composition ranges may introduce anomalies in model predictions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a systematic set of 10+ high-entropy alloy compositions spanning different principal elements and measure their melting temperatures, enthalpies, entropies, and volume changes using DSC and in-situ dilatometry. Compare the results to model predictions derived from the proposed hybrid approach.
measurements: Differential scanning calorimetry for melting temperature and enthalpy of fusion.
Precise density or dilatometry measurements up to and across the melting range.
Chemical composition verification (e.g., by X-ray fluorescence or inductively coupled plasma analysis) to ensure sample consistency.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If more than half of the tested alloys exhibit deviations exceeding ±10% in the predicted fusion enthalpy or ±10 K in melting temperature, the hybrid modeling and experimental calibration approach is considered invalidated.
